signals.description:
Gente do céu, que dias movimentados 🥵 Bora colocar o papo em dia? TL;DR Resumo do resumo das principais notícias da semana 🧠 Senado aprova o fim da escala 6x1 e a redução da jornada também para quem faz 5x2 . 🧠 Brasil regulamenta o Marco dos Games e anuncia apoio à produção nacional. 🧠 Instagram vai remover a opção de conectar Reels em séries. 🧠 Guia da Later mostra como incluir buscas por IA no planejamento com creators . 🧠 “Super like” aparece no LinkedIn . Temos prints. MANDA NEWS Novidades da semana. Senado aprova o fim da escala 6x1 no Brasil. Aqui tem o link com a curadoria do LinkedIn sobre o assunto . A IAB Brasil lançou a edição 2026 do guia de IA na publicidade digital . O governo federal regulamentou o Marco Legal dos Jogos Eletrônicos e anunciou medidas para apoiar a produção brasileira. Entre elas: Rouanet Games: apoio à captação de patrocínios para desenvolvimento de jogos Formação: previsão de cursos de graduação em cinco universidades federais Game Brasil: criação de uma plataforma pública e gratuita para divulgar jogos brasileiros Crédito: proposta de reduzir o valor mínimo e os juros dos empréstimos do Fundo Setorial do Audiovisual Roblox escolheu SP para a estreia internacional do Creator Showdown. SUBSTACK Substack liberou novos controles de feed: permite ajustar a frequência de vídeos, áudios e textos longos, silenciar palavras e definir tópicos de interesse. signals.title: How to measure if AI agents actually use your Design System
signals.description: What I learned from Christoph Hellmuth at our AI Jam on September 29 2026 Christoph Hellmuth is Design Engineering Manager for Design Systems at NordVPN . His team builds Aurora. That is the design system behind NordVPN and other Nord Security products. At our AI Jam he showed Open Design System Bench . It is an open source tool that measures how well AI agents follow your design system and gives you a score from 0 to 100. These are my notes from his session. 😱 The AGENTS.md was there and the models still built their own buttons Christoph’s team did what everyone recommends. Aurora ships an AGENTS.md. Then they measured what the models actually did with it. In 41 of 57 guided generations the models hand-rolled buttons, dialogs and toggles instead of using the design system they were told about. That is 72%. “It just invented a button, and honestly, we were quite shocked, because we were thinking, like, yeah, best practices, they work well.” Every model launch comes with a scoreboard like SWE-bench or Terminal-Bench. None of them checks whether an agent uses your Button instead of inventing one. That gap hurts when leadership asks what the 50 to 80 hours of AI readiness work brought. Without a number you only have a feeling. “Cool, so can you prove it? And you… well, we did all these best practices, but not really, and that’s not really what leadership wants to hear.” 🔍 Two tools: a free audit and a behavioral benchmark The static audit reads your repo. It costs nothing and took 5 to 10 seconds in Christoph’s live demo. It checks what you ship for agents such as AGENTS.md, llms.txt, skills and catalog quality. You get a score plus a list of what is missing. The behavioral benchmark lets an agent build real screens with your system in a fresh workspace. Then it grades the result. You can also run the audit against several systems at once. Christoph compared open source systems like Carbon, Primer, Base UI and MUI. Chakra scored highest with 70.5. “In this just static check of 10 seconds, it also gives you basically a to-do list, and you can now go into Jira, create the tickets for the next month.” The audit score is always the optimistic one. Ticking checkboxes is easy. The real score shows up once an agent has to use your system. 📝 Tasks describe intent and never the component The benchmark ships with 10 tasks. One example is a password reset screen. Another is the area where a user cancels a subscription. A task never names a component. Otherwise you only test whether the model can read. You can write your own tasks and weigh the rubric yourself. Christoph’s example: a red destructive cancel button can count for more than a support link. A built-in linter checks your task before you run it. In his demo it failed a task because the prompt mentioned the real export PasswordInput . 📊 What gets graded Each output is scored on six dimensions. The weights come from the README : imports (10%): Only your package, React and local files are imported apiFidelity (25%): No hallucinated components or invented props tokenDiscipline (15%): No raw hex values, arbitrary Tailwind or hardcoded styles a11yStatic (10%): Accessible names, labels and valid ARIA compile (10%): TypeScript compiles judgment (30%): Per-task rubric graded by a separate model By default every task runs 3 times per model. The worst run counts so the score never looks better than what a designer would get on a bad day. The hallucinations Christoph found in Aurora were very specific. Aurora has a heading prop and the model invented a Heading component. Aurora has Text and the model used Typography . It also invented spacing props on Box and Card. “They hand over the AI generated prototype to developers. And they tell you, well, we don’t really have any of these props, or this is an invented component.” 📉 The repo read 20 points better than it behaved Christoph ran the benchmark on Aurora AppKit. The audit gave it 64.8. Six models building with it scored 44.9. Only 10 of 55 guided cells compiled against the published types. The npm run produced about 250 type errors. About 100 of them came from direction="column" on a prop that only takes 'vertical' | 'horizontal' . The uncomfortable part: their own AGENTS.md and DESIGN.md mentioned a cn helper and a bare Radix component that never existed in the codebase. Their docs were teaching the agent some of the traps. 💡 One sentence in the README flipped it Their AGENTS.md told the model what not to use. In the run against the source code 72% of the buttons were still hand-rolled. Then they added one sentence to the README saying the package is installed. In the run against the npm package only 22% were hand-rolled. “Even things you thought, oh, this is useless, like, why should I tell the AI that my design system package is installed? No, it actually makes a difference.” After fixing the findings the audit score went from 64.8 to 82.0. The fixes included exporting the types nobody had exported and generating an llms.txt. He also tested six open models with and without an AGENTS.md. In the session he said adding one file moved the scores by 20 to 30 points. His write-up lists DeepSeek V4 Pro going from 58.7 to 84.8 and Sonnet 5 single-shot going from 51.2 to 75.3. 🛠️ How to run it on your design system The repo supports React and TypeScript libraries plus web components built with Stencil or Lit. Your system can be local source or an npm package. Clone open-design-system-bench Install and set it up: npm install npx tsx src/cli.ts init # wizard asks for package name, location and how you serve it npx tsx src/cli.ts doctor # checks your config and CLI setup npx tsx src/cli.ts extract # builds the component catalog npx tsx src/cli.ts run --profile smoke # 2 cells in about 5 minutes Run the bigger profiles once the smoke test passes. small has 5 cells for weekly checks and full has 90 cells for a quarterly baseline. You do not have to type any of this. Christoph and I both said it in the session: paste the repo link into Claude Code and ask it to install the benchmark and run it against your design system. A full run with Claude Code took him half an hour to an hour. His run with 6 models took about 3 hours. Watch the cost. Through the API a run with the top models can cost a few hundred dollars. A subscription is much cheaper. Christoph’s tip for the report: give it to Claude and ask for a PDF for leadership with an executive summary, the models tested, the results and the costs. 🎨 What about Figma? Vee asked in the Q&A whether you can score Figma and code together. Christoph’s answer: a Figma file alone mostly tests how well the AI uses the Figma MCP. It says little about your design system. His recommendation for the Figma to code workflow is Code Connect. “Honestly, at least from what we’ve seen, CodeConnect is totally worth having for, your Figma to code, workflow.” What I’m taking back to my own work These are my own takeaways and not Christoph’s: Run the free audit first. It takes seconds and gives you a ticket list. Never trust the audit score alone. Aurora lost 20 points once agents had to build with it. Tell the agent what to use and not only what to avoid. Grep your own AGENTS.md for helpers and components that do not exist. Write benchmark tasks the way a designer would brief a screen. Never name the component. Links from the session Open Design System Bench on GitHub Christoph’s write-up with all results Open Design System MCP : an MCP server from Christoph that exposes your real components and tokens to agents so they stop inventing names and props What Does AI-Readiness Mean in Design Systems? by Cristian Morales Design Engineer job in the Aurora team at Nord Security Watch Christoph’s full session and the live demo The recording of this AI Jam is part of the AI Design Systems Conference 2027 ticket. The conference runs online on March 10 and 11 2027 with speakers from Anthropic, OpenAI, Atlassian, Netflix and Yahoo. signals.title: #307 | Cronicamente offline
signals.description: nas edições anteriores #305 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 2) #306 | Uma seleção de campanhas tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 “A habilidade mais importante do próximo século não vai ser conectar humanos com mais tecnologia. Vai ser conectar humanos uns com os outros”. _ “Ninguém confia no gosto de quem só consome fast-food”. _ Em 2025, a WGSN já tinha previsto que a fadiga digital e o excesso de estímulos levaria as pessoas a migrarem para comunidades no mundo real: “Até 2027, a busca por menos barulho e mais desconexão digital vai ser o novo normal, emergindo como uma demonstração de autocuidado em forma de ambientes mais calmos, seguros e significativos” Isso tem se traduzido na realização e/ou incentivo de todo tipo de experiência. Um grande destaque no Brasil, que ilustra tanto o pertencimento quanto o autocuidado e, claro, a presença das marcas, são as corridas de rua. Segundo a Exame , em 2024 foram realizadas 2.827 corridas de rua oficiais no país. Em 2025, mais de 5 mil. Além disso, temos visto o crescimento de eventos em lojas, jantares especiais para clientes, clubes do livro, exibições em salas de cinema e convites para as mais diversas atividades físicas, manuais, intelectuais e sociais. E assim seguirá essa tendência - em 2027 e além. O que nos traz à edição de hoje é a sua relação com a creator economy . No que o Digiday chamou de “ vibes over metrics ”, os eventos presenciais agora são também uma estratégia de engajamento e construção de comunidade para marcas pessoais - ou marcas essencialmente virtuais. _ Três movimentos estão por trás disso: 1 - O mundo “pós-feed”, em que as redes sociais se tornaram oficialmente plataformas de descoberta e entretenimento, e onde “número de seguidores” é uma métrica cada vez menos determinante de sucesso e engajamento. Hoje, a viralização está muito mais ligada à adequação de um conteúdo a um nicho, assunto, tom ou formato (ou todos ao mesmo tempo). Mas quando encontrar uma audiência tem se tornado mais fácil, aprofundar essa relação é o desafio. Seja criando um universo de marca que gere reconhecimento e lembrança, seja reunindo essas pessoas para além do feed. 2 - A busca por mais presença , que é comum a todas as gerações e todos os nichos - todo mundo gostaria de ter mais atenção, mais concentração e mais serendipidade na vida. O que varia muito é como isso acontece. Quais rituais alguém pode incorporar ao seu dia a dia? Qual a periodicidade ideal desses encontros? Qual a atmosfera perfeita para proporcionar aquilo que alguém mais precisa? Assim como fazem com o seu conteúdo, seja lifestyle, seja desenvolvimento profissional, a curadoria e capacidade de simplificar informações dos creators tem muito valor aqui. O que nos traz ao próximo ponto. 3 - O tal do repertório, que nunca se falou tanto em construir, mas que não está nos mesmos vídeos ou carrosseis virais que todo mundo está compartilhando. Repertório é o que se traduz em uma perspectiva única que só aquela pessoa consegue trazer, com base em tudo que ela carrega consigo. Textos, imagens, experiências, tudo aquilo que você já viu e vivenciou, o lugar da onde você vem, os lugares por onde já passou, as boas conversas, os livros fáceis ou difíceis, os hábitos diários e ambientes que frequenta… Tudo isso forma o seu repertório. Que pode ser composto, sim, pelo que passa pelo feed e vai morar na sua pasta de “salvos” ou no mosaico mental de referências que você acessa a cada job. Mas um ponto de vista realmente original não vem de consumir mais do mesmo, ou apenas o que é filtrado por algoritmos. Vem de uma vida interessante o suficiente para influenciar tudo que você faz. Uma vida que acontece através de telas, mas principalmente fora delas. Naqueles ambientes em que conseguimos estar presentes com todo o nosso corpo (não apenas os nossos dedos em contato com uma tela fria). Naqueles momentos em que uma informação é registrada não porque é vista, mas porque é vivida, com todas as nuances do ambiente, das pessoas que estão ali e de como ela é apresentada. No conhecimento que alguém realmente tem para passar - sem ferramentas que escrevem roteiros, sem a chance de regravar até ficar bom o suficiente. Nas trocas que a gente não consegue pensar antes de digitar ou gravar duas ou três vezes antes de enviar. Depois de anos cronicamente online, é por essas e outras que o conteúdo, a influência e as comunidades têm buscado o offline. _ Quando “comunidade” era a grande tendência nos relatórios, a gente se tornava uma. Quando carrosséis anunciavam o retorno das revistas impressas, a nossa já estava na gráfica. Quando certos produtos físicos estavam virando colecionáveis, o nosso boné esgotou em 24 horas. Agora, chegou a vez da gente olhar para o offline - como movimento de mercado e necessidade humana - do único jeito que a gente sabe fazer: ✨ na prática ✨ Topam ser uma comunidade presencial também? :) Nosso encontro está marcado no dia 27 de outubro, terça-feira, na Avenida Paulista. Com direito a revista impressa e convidados mais que especiais. As vagas são limitadas, e o cupom NEWSLETTER dá 15% de desconto para as dez primeiras pessoas vindas aqui da news: vem para o Bits Ao Vivo para inspirar ✨ A marca americana Altra Running anunciou o seu Altra Legacy Team - a equipe de corrida mais velha do mundo. Juntos, eles têm 321 anos de idade. E querem provar que o objetivo não é correr mais rápido. E sim, seguir correndo. O vídeo do making of da campanha é sensacional. para fazer parte da conversa 💬 O resultado do primeiro turno das eleições foi um grande chá revelação de que vivemos em bolhas. Imprevisível pelas pesquisas, ele demonstrou o retorno do fenômeno “22 confirma”, que elegeu candidatos de postura e currículo extremamente questionáveis sob o guarda-chuva do bolsonarismo. Para refletir sobre o voto que ainda temos a dar neste segundo turno: Quem ocupa as cadeiras do Legislativo em 2027 , uma análise em gráficos Bolsonarismo ou anti-petismo? , um episódio do podcast Café da Manhã A Guerra à Santa , mini-documentário sobre a história (e politização) de Nossa Senhora Aparecida _ “ Cutewashing ”. A Meta e a OpenAI lançaram agentes de IA com nomes e identidades visuais muito fofas. Isso é um estudo de caso de branding, de como a forma com que uma tecnologia é apresentada faz toda diferença em como ela será adotada pelas pessoas. Voltaremos no assunto em breve, mas para quem quiser abrir algumas abas desde já: Por que as big tech querem que agentes de IA sejam os novos labubu Empresas de tecnologia lançam mascotes fofos para aliviar a ansiedade com a IA para continuar a conversa nas redes sociais e convidar mais gente para cá, compartilhe usando o botão abaixo ou marcando a @bitstobrands Share para ler com calma 📄 A gente costumava fazer logoff Diretamente do Pinterest, relatório de tendências em beleza e tendências em hobbies Precisamos olhar para o Brasil mesmo quando é difícil “Não acredito em celebrar o país apenas quando o mundo lá fora está falando bem da gente. Acho que nosso compromisso é outro. É estudar o Brasil e tentar compreendê-lo, embora talvez nunca consigamos inteiramente. É um exercício constante”. para mais conteúdo 📚 🖼️ siga a Bits no Instagram [link] 📚 confira uma seleção de livros na nossa biblioteca [link] 🎧 ouça o podcast Tudo que Importa [link] 🤝 anuncie na Bits - peça o nosso mídia kit em contato@bitstobrands.com 📩 assine essa newsletter , caso não tenha recebido por e-mail :) Subscribe now para dar um tchau 👋🏼 Semana passada, em Vitória, um grupo animado de leitoras da Bits pediu uma foto depois de uma palestra. Sorrindo, uma delas se aproximou dizendo “eu sou muito fã, eu acompanho a newsletter desde quando era você que escrevia!!!”. Eu imagino que essa impressão vem do fato de que a Bits agora tem um time, e tem muito mais projetos e canais do que quando eu comecei uma newsletter nas madrugadas CLT. Mas esse espaço bem aqui, na sua caixa de entrada, onde tudo começou, é pra onde eu faço questão de voltar. Pessoalmente, sem assistente de IA, digitando cada palavra. É tão escrita por mim no alto das suas 307 edições, que a sua frequência está tão maluca quanto a rotina de idas e vindas pelo aeoporto de Congonhas. Mas eu sempre volto. Nem que seja com uma leitura para o fim de semana :) E, claro, um convite mais que especial! - Bia

visualFeast.title: Snøhetta completes landmark opera house in Shanghai
visualFeast.description: A giant spiral staircase guides visitors to the roof of the Shanghai Grand Opera House, which international studio Snøhetta designed to be "as much a civic destination as a performance venue". Located on the Huangpu River waterfront in Shanghai, China, the 146,786-square-metre opera house was conceived as a major cultural landmark that can accommodate a variety of musical performances. Snøhetta has completed the Shanghai Grand Opera House While Snøhetta 's design responds to a highly ambitious brief, the studio said it began the project as it always does, by taking time to examine and understand the specific site and its context, no matter the scale. According to the studio, this helped it to create the desired landmark while ensuring it felt like an extension of the existing public realm, open and accessible to both ticket holders and passersby. It is located on the Huangpu River waterfront "We always begin the same way, regardless of scale: by understanding the context," Snøhetta co-founder Kjetil Thorsen told Dezeen. "A cultural building, any building for that matter, must respond to its surroundings, the people who use it, the performers it serves, and the city it becomes part of," he reflected. "When I last visited the site, I was asked by a Chinese architecture student how we managed to create a building that felt so Chinese despite not being from China. The answer lies in observation and understanding context." Its key feature is a giant spiral staircase Shanghai Grand Opera House's defining feature is its spiral staircase, which dramatically cantilevers at its peak and was intended to emulate everything from an unfolding fan to a dancer or a set of piano keys. It leads directly to the publicly accessible rooftop, which doubles as a stage, an observation deck or simply a meeting point. According to Thorsen, it was integral to making the building feel part of the urban fabric. The staircase has a dramatic cantilever He compared the design to the Oslo Opera House , which the studio completed in 2000, with both designs actively seeking to "reduce thresholds wherever possible". "Buildings like opera houses inevitably create thresholds through walls, doors, and ticketed programs. We see it as our responsibility to challenge those thresholds and make the building as much a civic destination as a performance venue," Thorsen explained. "People should be able to enjoy the building without attending a performance. It should become part of everyday life, a place to spend time, meet others, and experience the city," he added. "A successful landmark is not only recognised by visitors, it is also embraced by the people who live around it and make it part of their everyday lives." The lobby is designed to feel light and open Shanghai Grand Opera House has a radial plan and contains a trio of auditoriums alongside exhibition and education spaces, restaurants and rehearsal and production areas. The facade flits between transparent and opaque finishes, depending on where the studio wanted to provide privacy and openness. For example, expansive glass elements maximise natural light and views in the lobby. The main auditorium has five levels Together, the three auditoriums can accommodate 4,200 people and host a range of performances. The main auditorium, called the Harmony Hall, contains 2,000 seats across its five levels, while the second hall, named the Soar Theatre, is more intimate, with space for 1,200 people. The final auditorium contains 1,000 seats and was constructed as a highly flexible space with adaptive seating and staging, catering to more experimental performances. It is fronted with a large glass facade overlooking the river. "For younger generations especially, that flexibility can help make cultural experiences feel more relevant, accessible, and connected to contemporary life," said Thorsen. Read: Snøhetta's Oslo Opera House was the most significant building of 2007 Shanghai Grand Opera House's material palette is a play of contrasts, with the light-coloured white stone, glass, and timber exterior having a more open feel than the darker, more intimate interiors. Inside, the auditoriums each have a unique aesthetic. The main hall is filled with deep red tones and surfaces, intended to feel as though they are carved from a single block, while lighter wooden materials characterise the other two. At night, the stage towers that project from the building are illuminated, shifting in colour to "animate the roof and the skyline". The smallest performance hall is designed to be adaptive Minimising the building's carbon footprint was a significant challenge due to the building's "scale and complexity", Thorsen said, but this was achieved through measures including passive design strategies. The bright roof reflects sunlight and heat rather than absorbing it, and the public lobby opens towards both the river and the park, allowing for cross-ventilation. A palette of durable materials and an adaptable interior will ensure a long lifespan for the building, while a close connection to public transport minimises dependence on private vehicles. Shanghai Grand Opera House is complete with a landscape design that connects to existing parkland, wetlands and public spaces to support local biodiversity and provide ample public space. The other auditorium accommodates 1,200 guests Snøhetta was founded by Thorsen and Craig Dykers in 1989. It won an international competition to design the opera house in 2016 and developed it with the state-owned firm East China Architectural Design & Research Institute (ECADI) and consultants Theatre Projects and Nagata Acoustics . Other major cultural projects by the studio include the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in North Dakota and the rippled Glasshouse Theatre in Queensland . The photography is by Yumeng Zhu , Tian Fangfang , Chen Hao and StudioSZ . The post Snøhetta completes landmark opera house in Shanghai appeared first on Dezeen .

Tesla launches flying Roadster concept car
visualFeast.description: Electric car company Tesla has unveiled its flying Roadster vehicle with a demonstration in which the car drove upside down, flipped off a ramp and briefly flew, using compressed-air thrusters that Tesla claims will make it the world's quickest production car. During a live event in Texas, the two-seat Roadster model drove up a half-pipe ramp and launched off the top, remaining in the air for a few seconds before landing It also became airborne after building up speed on flat ground, launching over a row of parked vehicles. It then lifted off from a stationary position. Tesla has unveiled its second-generation Roadster A series of thrusters in the bottom and back propelled the car into the air and cushioned the landings. It was designed by Tesla and SpaceX, both companies led by businessman Elon Musk, who called the second-generation Roadster "a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company". It has thrusters that use compressed air The thrusters can also fire rearward to boost acceleration. Tesla demonstrated the car reaching 60 miles per hour in a claimed 0.81 seconds, and said it would be the "quickest" production vehicle to 60 miles per hour. On the half-pipe ramp, the vehicle was able to remain upside down due to a fan suction system. The air tanks in the vehicle are rechargeable and can be recompressed without fuel, according to Tesla. The vehicle uses compressed air to take off and land Long term, Musk said the car will be the "only manual" vehicle in its lineup, referencing plans for driverless vehicles . Though the demonstration used a pre-programmed sequence with no driver. Tesla chief designer Franz von Holzhausen said the car was designed with an "aerospace aesthetic". It has an angular supercar exterior with scissor doors and a deployable spoiler, and is a coupe with a hard top. Read: Videos reveal vertical takeoff of electric flying car in California The seats are moulded directly to the chassis, and it features wire steering, which replaces the mechanical link between the steering wheel and wheels with electronic controls. Musk referenced the uncertainty of street legality for the flying capabilities and said that " success is not guaranteed" before the test. The company gave it an "aerospace aesthetic" Production on the vehicle is set for 2028, according to Tesla. The company first unveiled a second-generation Roadster in 2017 , with deliveries planned for 2020. Tesla's last major launch was the Cybertruck , unveiled in 2019. Other recent concept cars include Alef's concept vehicle . The imagery is courtesy of Tesla. The post Tesla launches flying Roadster concept car appeared first on Dezeen .
